summary:
Research when running a model on a user device is technically and economically appropriate, and when cloud or hybrid execution is preferable. Focus on representative smartphones, personal computers, and a constrained edge-device class rather than attempting to catalogue all hardware. Use public evidence from 2023 through 2026-11-09, with earlier technical foundations where necessary. The evidence cutoff is 2026-11-09; identify hardware configurations, model releases, runtimes, and measurement versions, and distinguish shipping capabilities from announced support.

Explain the constraints that determine deployability: available memory rather than installed memory alone, weight storage, runtime working memory, KV-cache growth, memory bandwidth, supported operations, CPU/GPU/NPU scheduling, power draw, thermal throttling, and sustained latency. Separate prefill from decoding, time to first output from throughput, and short demonstrations from repeated or continuous use. Explain why nominal accelerator throughput or a model fitting in storage does not by itself establish useful end-to-end performance.

Compare model sizes and architectures, quantization, compression or distillation, context-management strategies, and relevant runtime optimizations. Discuss which changes reduce memory, bandwidth, or compute demands and what accuracy or task-quality degradation accompanies them. Do not assume that lower numerical precision automatically improves speed on every device. Separate evidence for text workloads from evidence for speech or vision pipelines, including preprocessing and non-model components where they materially affect latency or energy.

Use task-driven comparisons covering private document assistance, interactive text generation, and a continuous or frequently invoked speech or vision function. Select public model–hardware combinations with enough information to explain their suitability. Build deployment envelopes with explicit units and assumptions for memory, context, latency, and power where evidence permits. Preserve differences in task difficulty, output length, batch size, decoding configuration, and quality targets; unlike vendor measurements should not be normalized into a single ranking without justification. Missing measurements can be represented as bounded scenarios or unresolved constraints, not fabricated benchmarks.

Analyze local-only, cloud-only, and hybrid execution for these tasks. Include network availability and latency, transfer size, privacy and data retention, fallback behavior, model updates, operating-system restrictions, and the integration burden of heterogeneous devices. Explain where local processing changes the privacy boundary and where logging, synchronization, or cloud fallback reintroduces data exposure. Evaluate total task cost and user experience rather than treating the absence of a per-token API charge as zero cost.

Deliver a complete research report with a hardware–model–task fit matrix, worked deployment envelopes, and conditional edge–cloud design recommendations. Give concrete decision rules for offline use, sensitive data, bursty high-complexity requests, and sustained background workloads. Tables and text diagrams may be placed wherever they support the argument; no fixed chapter structure is required.

The main checks are whether performance claims retain their measurement conditions, whether peak and sustained performance remain distinct, and whether quality degradation and integration constraints are included in the recommendation. Treat vendor demonstrations, independent tests, and estimated envelopes as different types of evidence. A conclusion favoring the cloud, a narrowly scoped local model, or a hybrid architecture is equally acceptable when it follows from the workload and hardware conditions.
